text:
This section documents the data sources behind the ready-to-use product definitions maintained in the official Open Data Cube datacube-dataset-config repository — the default catalog available to any Open Data Cube deployment. Each data source has its own dedicated page below.


Landsat — Collection 2 Level-2 Science Products
Sentinel — Sentinel-1 (radar) and Sentinel-2 (optical) missions
Planetary Computer — STAC catalog used to access several of these sources
NASADEM — global elevation model
Copernicus DEM — European/global elevation model, alternative to NASADEM
ESA WorldCover — global land cover at 10 m
Impact Observatory Land Cover — annual global land use/land cover







Note



The Nostradamus datacube uses most of these default products, but under different, project-specific names, and adds a couple of sources that are not part of the default catalog. See Data sources used in the Nostradamus datacube for the mapping.

title: Data cubes installation
text: Installing a data cube involves two main phases. The first is setting up the underlying software and infrastructure on the machine that will host the cube, typically a server (on-premises or cloud-based) or, for testing and development, a local computer or virtual machine: installing system libraries for handling geospatial formats (GDAL, HDF5, netCDF), a Python environment with the Open Data Cube (ODC) package, and a PostgreSQL/PostGIS database that will hold the index of all available data.

title: What is a data cube?
text: Earth observation missions such as Landsat, Sentinel, and MODIS now provide multi-decade, continuously growing archives of satellite imagery, but this data has traditionally been organised and distributed scene by scene, requiring heavy preprocessing before it can be compared or combined across dates and sensors. A data cube addresses this bottleneck: it provides a common framework to catalogue, access, and analyse large volumes of gridded Earth observation data so that routine, reliable, and reproducible analyses, rather than one-off scene processing, can support evidence-based decisions in areas such as environmental monitoring, agriculture, and land management.

title: Nostradamus datacube installation
text:
Note



A detailed installation procedure and other admin and user tutorials exist. The steps below consist in additional help to the links mentioned for a Docker install of the Nostradamus data cube



Docker

Install Docker desktop for your operating system and launch it
To make sure all works fine, type the following commands in your Terminal (example on Mac OS):

docker –-version 
and
docker compose version
If corresponding information is returned, it means all is working fine for your Docker session and you can proceed to the next steps






Caution



At this stage, don’t start yet any Docker container




Terminal

Clone the Nostradamus jupyter cube into your local Docker application by typing the following command:

git clone https://git.unepgrid.ch/NOSTRADAMUS/cube-in-a-box-jupyter.git
This will create a cube-in-a-box-jupyter folder with all the necessary Docker files. In case the folder already exists, use the pull command (more info in the FAQ page)

Once the installation is finalized, go to the newly created folder by typing in your Terminal

cd cube-in-a-box-jupyter

After a first install, you need to setup the environment variables (in the .env file). To do so, you need first to copy the existing default .env file by typing

cp .env.default .env

As both the original .env.default and copied .env files are hidden files, you need to activate the hidden files display in your system (e.g. Cmd + Shift + . in Mac finder)
Open then the .env file you copied (for example in a text editor) and add a user (for example your first name) with an admin role in the line JUPYTERHUB_ADMINS, adding a comma after “admin”



Restart JupyterHub to take these changes into account

docker-compose restart jupyterhub


Use then the make setup command to initiate the datacube before using it. You can either simply type make setup, which will deploy the datacube with all layers available, or you can filter a specific area of interest using the BBOX parameter (e.g. make setup BBOX=5.95,45.81,10.50,47.81) and the DATETIME parameter specifying a particular time range (e.g. make setup BBOX=5.95,45.81,10.50,47.81 DATETIME=2024-01-01/2024-12-31)

Your Terminal should be showing activity


Web browser

Go to http://localhost/explorer/products to check if all is working fine. If it is the case, you should see an image like the one below



Go to http://localhost/jupyter and click on signup to create a new user corresponding to the one you have attributed the admin role in point 7.



In the next screen, enter this user and give a password. If all works fine, you should see a confirmation message saying that the signup was successful.







Note



Do not forget to write down your username and password as these will be needed for later login for using the data cube



On this same screen, click on the login link and log in with the credentials you just created. If all works fine, you should reach in your browser the homepage of the JupyterHub interface of the Nostradamus datacube.


If you check your Docker desktop instance, a container with a name containing “cube-in-a-box” should be running.






Tip



the url to reach your the homepage of the JupyterHub interface of the Nostradamus datacube should be localhost/jupyter/user/[username]/lab

title: UNIGE & UNEP/GRID-Geneva data cubes Capacity Building
text:
This site is a capacity-building resource on data cubes and Earth observation, developed by UNIGE and UNEP/GRID-Geneva. It introduces the core concepts behind data cubes: which problems they help to solve, how they organise satellite and geospatial data, and the main steps involved in setting them up. It also allows to walk through concrete, hands-on implementations.
At its core is the Nostradamus datacube, a modified Open Data Cube deployment with a multi-user JupyterHub, an integrated STAC datastore, and ready-to-use notebooks. The site documents how to install and use it, complemented by step-by-step tutorials, recorded workshops, and a parallel section on vector datacubes for non-raster geospatial data.
Beyond the datacube itself, the site catalogues the underlying data sources (Landsat, Sentinel, the Planetary Computer STAC catalog) and the tools used to work with them (Jupyter, LivingEarth), along with acknowledgments and a FAQ for troubleshooting. Use the sidebar to navigate by topic, or start with the Introduction to datacubes for a general overview before diving into the Nostradamus-specific material.

title: Nostradamus datacube
text: This work is part of Work Package 5 (WP5) – Development & Implementation of Data Cubes of the Nostradamus project, led by the University of Geneva. WP5 aims to provide guidance for producing rasterized data from sources such as satellite imagery and existing geospatial databases for effective ingestion into Data Cubes, to develop a dedicated Data Cube for each participating country’s agricultural case study area, and to implement an exploitation platform built on these Data Cubes. It integrates satellite sensor, in-situ, and ancillary data, defining entry points for real-time streams, environmental datasets, and spatiotemporal data cubes, building on synergies with related initiatives such as the LandShift project to share infrastructure and mutualize development efforts. The resulting platform provides demo notebooks by default, lets users download new data and index scenes using STAC, and makes newly ingested data immediately visible for exploration in the Data Cube explorer.

title: Landsat
text:
Landsat collections
The Landsat archive of raw and processed data since 1972 is organized into 3 collections:

Pre-collection (before 2016): old on-demand processing system, no longer available
Collection 1 (2016-2022): tiered collection management structure, ensuring that all Landsat Level-1 products provide a consistent archive of known data quality to support time-series analyses and data “stacking”. No longer available
Collection 2 (2022-present): reprocessing of the Collection 1 archive resulting in several product improvements that harness recent advancements in data processing, algorithm development, and data access and distribution capabilities: alignment of the pixels, sensors value coherence, metadata quality, etc to have a more accurate product

title: Landsat
text:
Landsat levels
Each collection organises data into levels of processing:

Level1 (L1): raw data corrected for geometry and topography
Level2 (L2): L1 images are taken as the basis, on which physical values of the atmosphere (aerosols, ozone, water vapor, …) are corrected => ready data for certain analyses (indices calculation, multi-temporal series, etc.) that could not be done with L1 images
Level3 (L3): analytical derived products from L2, that are automatically generated

title: How to index new data into a DC?
text:
Once a datacube is deployed, the Earth observation archive keeps growing: new satellite scenes become available over time and need to be added to the existing index so they can be queried and analysed alongside the rest of the archive. Since the Nostradamus datacube uses a STAC datastore (the Planetary Computer catalog) as its data source, new scenes do not need to be prepared or described by hand: they can be indexed directly from the STAC catalog into an existing product.
In short, the procedure consists of searching the STAC catalog for new scenes matching a product, an area of interest, and a date range, then registering the matching STAC items into the corresponding ODC product already configured in the cube. This is done with the stac-to-dc command-line tool (part of odc-apps-dc-tools), which is already installed in the Nostradamus JupyterHub environment. Once indexed, the new scenes are immediately visible in the ODC Explorer and loadable through the Python API, exactly like the rest of the archive.

title: STAC datastore
text:
STAC stands for “SpatioTemporal Asset Catalog”. It is an OGC open standard for organizing and facilitating discoverability and access to geospatial and remote sensing data through a standardized metadata structure and query.
A “spatiotemporal asset” is any file that represents information about the Earth (satellite image, LiDAR data, meteorological data, …) at a certain place and time.
Among other advantages, a STAC datastore allows to:

Discover data without downloading a dataset
Filter by geographic zone, data range, cloud cover, …
Interoperate between different platforms (AWS, Google Earth Engine, Copernicus,…)
Access the files directly (Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFF, COG, …)

Specific tools have been developed to interact with STAC datastore, such as:

pystac: Python library to manipulate STAC catalogues
QGIS STAC plugin: allows to navigate in STAC catalogs from QGIS

title: Glossary
text:
A free, open-source software package that simplifies the management and analysis of large amounts of satellite imagery and other Earth observation data. It allows users to easily access, process, and analyze decades of geographical data to track changes on Earth’s surface over time.
https://www.opendatacube.org

title: Glossary
text:
STAC
SpatioTemporal Asset Catalog (STAC) is a common specification for describing geospatial data (satellite imagery, aerial imagery, and other Earth observation data) in a way that makes it easily searchable and interoperable across catalogues, tools, and platforms. A STAC catalogue organizes data into Items (individual assets with spatial/temporal metadata) grouped into Collections, all described using a standardized JSON schema.
https://stacspec.org

title: Glossary
text:
Cloud Optimized GeoTIFF
Cloud Optimized GeoTIFF (COG) is a regular GeoTIFF file, aimed at being hosted on a cloud storage service (e.g., object storage such as AWS S3 or Azure Blob Storage), whose internal organization (tiling, overviews) enables efficient partial reads via HTTP range requests. This means clients can access only the portion of the image they need without downloading the entire file, which is essential for scalable, on-demand access to large Earth Observation datasets.
https://www.cogeo.org

title: Glossary
text:
Analysis Ready Data

Analysis Ready Data (ARD) refers to satellite (or other remote sensing) data that has been processed to a minimum set of requirements — such as geometric correction, atmospheric correction, and consistent formatting — so that it can be used directly for analysis with minimal additional preprocessing. ARD reduces the technical burden on end users and improves comparability and interoperability across datasets, sensors, and time periods.

title: Glossary
text:
Common Workflow Language
Common Workflow Language (CWL) is an open standard for describing analysis workflows and tools in a way that makes them portable and scalable across different software and hardware environments (e.g., workstations, clusters, cloud platforms). CWL is commonly used to package and execute Earth Observation processing pipelines in a reproducible, containerized manner.
https://www.commonwl.org

title: Glossary
text:
REST
Representational State Transfer (REST) is an architectural style for designing networked, web-based APIs. A REST API exposes resources (e.g., datasets, catalogue entries, processing results) through standard HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) and uniform, predictable URLs, typically exchanging data in formats such as JSON. REST APIs are widely used to enable interoperable, machine-readable access to data and services, including within data cube and STAC-based infrastructures.

title: What is a data cube?
text: Earth observation missions such as Landsat, Sentinel, and MODIS now provide multi-decade, continuously growing archives of satellite imagery, but this data has traditionally been organised and distributed scene by scene, requiring heavy preprocessing before it can be compared or combined across dates and sensors. A data cube addresses this bottleneck: it provides a common framework to catalogue, access, and analyse large volumes of gridded Earth observation data so that routine, reliable, and reproducible analyses, rather than one-off scene processing, can support evidence-based decisions in areas such as environmental monitoring, agriculture, and land management.

title: What is a data cube?
text:
What a data cube is
Technically, a data cube is an open-source geospatial data management and analysis platform (the Open Data Cube (ODC) being the most widely adopted implementation) that organises satellite imagery and other gridded data (elevation models, geophysical grids, model outputs) along space, time, and spectral dimensions. Unlike traditional scene-based approaches, every observation is preserved individually, enabling a shift from scene-based to pixel-based analysis. It exposes this data through a Python API, a catalogue of indexed products, and complementary tools such as the Open Data Cube Explorer, Jupyter notebooks, and OGC web services.

title: What is a data cube?
text:
Setting up a data cube
Setting up a data cube typically follows a few main steps: selecting and deploying the underlying infrastructure (local, HPC, or cloud) and installing the ODC software stack; defining the interfaces and standards used to describe the data, such as STAC and OGC web services; preparing and indexing the data (usually Analysis Ready Data (ARD)) as datasets and products with standardised metadata; and building a catalogue for discovery, along with the tools (explorer, notebooks, APIs) needed to query, process, and exploit the cube.

title: What is a data cube?
text:
Existing data cube deployments
Several operational data cubes now build on this open-source foundation at different scales, including the Swiss Data Cube, jointly operated by the University of Geneva, UNEP/GRID-Geneva, the University of Zurich, and the WSL; Digital Earth Africa, delivering continental-scale Earth observation services across Africa; and Digital Earth Australia, run by Geoscience Australia to track more than 30 years of landscape change. The Nostradamus datacube presented in this site follows the same approach, adapted to the project’s agricultural case studies.
Beyond the Open Data Cube itself, other platforms exist for managing and analysing large volumes of Earth observation data (see Other datacube platforms for an overview).

title: Nostradamus datacube
text: This work is part of Work Package 5 (WP5) – Development & Implementation of Data Cubes of the Nostradamus project, led by the University of Geneva. WP5 aims to provide guidance for producing rasterized data from sources such as satellite imagery and existing geospatial databases for effective ingestion into Data Cubes, to develop a dedicated Data Cube for each participating country’s agricultural case study area, and to implement an exploitation platform built on these Data Cubes. It integrates satellite sensor, in-situ, and ancillary data, defining entry points for real-time streams, environmental datasets, and spatiotemporal data cubes, building on synergies with related initiatives such as the LandShift project to share infrastructure and mutualize development efforts. The resulting platform provides demo notebooks by default, lets users download new data and index scenes using STAC, and makes newly ingested data immediately visible for exploration in the Data Cube explorer.

title: Data cubes installation
text: Installing a data cube involves two main phases. The first is setting up the underlying software and infrastructure on the machine that will host the cube, typically a server (on-premises or cloud-based) or, for testing and development, a local computer or virtual machine: installing system libraries for handling geospatial formats (GDAL, HDF5, netCDF), a Python environment with the Open Data Cube (ODC) package, and a PostgreSQL/PostGIS database that will hold the index of all available data.

title: Data cubes installation
text:
Populating the cube
Once the software stack is running and connected to its database, the second phase consists of populating the cube: describing the data to be added through product definitions and dataset documents, then indexing it so it becomes searchable and accessible through the ODC API and tools. Indexing only records metadata about the data; it does not copy, move, or transform the underlying files, making the process fast and safe to repeat.

title: CLMS CLC+ Backbone
text:
CLC+ Backbone is a land cover product from the Copernicus Land Monitoring Service (CLMS), providing a high-resolution (10 m) classification of Europe’s land surface, produced from Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 imagery. It complements the long-running CORINE Land Cover (CLC) inventory — which has a coarser resolution and a slower update cycle — by offering a more frequently refreshed, more spatially detailed backbone layer that CLC and other derived Copernicus land products build upon.
Being Europe-specific and higher resolution than global products like ESA WorldCover, CLC+ Backbone is well suited to regional or national-scale agricultural and land-management analyses within the EU, including several of the Nostradamus demonstration sites.

title: AlphaEarth Foundations embeddings
text:
AlphaEarth Foundations is a geospatial AI model developed by Google DeepMind, released in 2025, that produces annual “satellite embeddings”: for each 10 m pixel on Earth’s surface, it condenses information from multiple satellite and geospatial data sources (optical, radar, elevation, climate, and more) into a compact numerical vector. Unlike a conventional dataset that stores a physical measurement (a reflectance value, a temperature), an embedding stores a learned representation designed to be reused across many different downstream mapping and classification tasks (e.g., land cover, ecosystem mapping, change detection) without having to reprocess the original raw sources each time.
This is a substantially different kind of “data source” compared to the other products in this list — it is not a physical measurement but a machine-learning representation, distributed as Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFFs and mirrored on Source Cooperative.

title: Sentinel
text:
Sentinel is the family of Earth observation satellites operated by the European Union’s Copernicus programme. Two of these missions are the most commonly used sources in data cube deployments:

Sentinel-1: a radar (SAR, Synthetic Aperture Radar) mission, which measures the Earth’s surface independently of daylight and cloud cover. It is well suited to monitoring soil moisture, flooding, and surface deformation.
Sentinel-2: an optical, multispectral mission (13 bands), providing imagery well suited to vegetation monitoring, land cover mapping, and agricultural applications, but — unlike Sentinel-1 — affected by cloud cover.

Both missions provide free, openly accessible data with a revisit time of a few days, and are frequently used, alone or in combination, to derive higher-level products (such as ESA WorldCover or the CLC+ Backbone) rather than being used only as raw imagery.

title: How to index new data into a DC?
text:
Once a datacube is deployed, the Earth observation archive keeps growing: new satellite scenes become available over time and need to be added to the existing index so they can be queried and analysed alongside the rest of the archive. Since the Nostradamus datacube uses a STAC datastore (the Planetary Computer catalog) as its data source, new scenes do not need to be prepared or described by hand: they can be indexed directly from the STAC catalog into an existing product.
In short, the procedure consists of searching the STAC catalog for new scenes matching a product, an area of interest, and a date range, then registering the matching STAC items into the corresponding ODC product already configured in the cube. This is done with the stac-to-dc command-line tool (part of odc-apps-dc-tools), which is already installed in the Nostradamus JupyterHub environment. Once indexed, the new scenes are immediately visible in the ODC Explorer and loadable through the Python API, exactly like the rest of the archive.
The steps below index new Landsat Collection 2 Level-2 scenes into the existing lsX_c2l2_sp product (see the Landsat page) as a concrete example.
crumbs: How to index new data into a DC?

title: How to index new data into a DC?
text:
Indexing new Landsat scenes: step-by-step

Open a Terminal in the Nostradamus JupyterHub (File > New > Terminal), where datacube and stac-to-dc are already available.
Check that the target product is already registered in the cube:
datacube product list | grep lsX_c2l2_sp
Search the Planetary Computer STAC catalog for new scenes and index them directly into that product, specifying the collection, an area of interest (bounding box), and a date range:
stac-to-dc \
  --catalog-href="https://planetarycomputer.microsoft.com/api/stac/v1/" \
  --collections="landsat-c2-l2" \
  --bbox="5.95,45.81,10.50,47.81" \
  --datetime="2026-01-01/2026-06-30" \
  --rename-product="lsX_c2l2_sp" \
  --update-if-exists
--rename-product maps the STAC collection (landsat-c2-l2) to the existing ODC product name (lsX_c2l2_sp), and --bbox/--datetime restrict the search to the area and period you need (adjust them to your own area of interest).







Note



Planetary Computer assets are served through short-lived signed URLs. If loading newly indexed scenes later fails with an access error, see the STAC datastore page for how signing is handled, or re-run the indexing step to refresh the references.



Check the command’s output: it reports how many datasets were added, failed, and skipped (already-indexed scenes are skipped, not duplicated).
Confirm the new scenes are indexed by checking the product’s extent in the ODC Explorer, at localhost/explorer/products/lsX_c2l2_sp: the temporal coverage should now include your new date range.
Alternatively, confirm it directly from a notebook using the Python API:
from datacube import Datacube

dc = Datacube(app="check-new-data")
data = dc.load(product="lsX_c2l2_sp", time=("2026-01-01", "2026-06-30"))
print(data.time.values)

title: Impact Observatory Land Cover
text:
This dataset, produced by Impact Observatory in partnership with Esri and Microsoft, provides a global land use / land cover (LULC) classification derived from Sentinel-2 imagery using a deep-learning model, generated on an annual basis (rather than a single static reference year, unlike products such as ESA WorldCover). It classifies the land surface into 9 broad classes (e.g., water, trees, crops, built area, bare ground).
Because it is updated yearly, this product is particularly useful for tracking land use change year over year — for example monitoring the conversion of cropland to built-up area, or the expansion/contraction of cultivated land across a growing season sequence.

title: NASADEM

title: Other datacube platforms
text:
The Open Data Cube (ODC) is the most widely adopted open-source implementation of the data cube approach, and the one this site focuses on, but it is not the only platform for managing and analysing large volumes of Earth observation data. Depending on needs (self-hosted vs. cloud, open-source vs. commercial, raster-focused vs. general array data), several alternatives exist:

Google Earth Engine (GEE): a cloud-based, commercial platform with hundreds of datasets pre-integrated and a free tier for research/non-commercial use. Unlike the ODC, it is a closed, hosted service but it requires no infrastructure setup.
Sentinel Hub: a commercial web service for accessing and processing Copernicus (Sentinel) and other satellite imagery on demand, widely used for quick visualisation and lightweight processing without managing an archive.
rasdaman (and the related EarthServer initiative): an open-source array database management system, following OGC standards, that manages multidimensional data more generally (not only Earth observation imagery).
xcube: an open-source, Python/xarray-based toolkit (developed by Brockmann Consult) for building and analysing spatiotemporal data cubes, with a strong focus on Earth system science and Zarr-based cloud storage.
SEPAL: a cloud platform developed by the FAO for satellite data access, processing, and analysis, oriented towards land monitoring and forestry applications.
openEO: not a platform in itself, but a standardised API that exposes a common “virtual data cube” interface across several of the backends above, allowing the same analysis code to run on different providers.

title: Open Data Cube (ODC) — Overview
text: The Open Data Cube (ODC) is an open-source software project that provides the core framework used to build data cubes: it turns collections of individual satellite scenes and other gridded data into an analysis-ready, queryable archive organised along space, time, and spectral dimensions. ODC is not a single hosted service, it is a set of libraries and tools that anyone can deploy on their own infrastructure, which is why it underpins many independent deployments worldwide, from national platforms such as Digital Earth Australia and Digital Earth Africa to project-specific instances such as the Nostradamus datacube.

ODC is not a single hosted service, it is a set of libraries and tools that anyone can deploy on their own infrastructure, which is why it underpins many independent deployments worldwide, from national platforms such as Digital Earth Australia and Digital Earth Africa to project-specific instances such as the Nostradamus datacube.

title: Open Data Cube (ODC) — Overview
text:
Core components

datacube-core : the Python library and command-line tool at the heart of ODC. It manages the index (what data is available and where), handles product and dataset definitions, and provides the Python API used to load and analyse data.
PostgreSQL/PostGIS index: the database that stores metadata about every indexed dataset (spatial extent, time, format, location of the underlying files). Indexing only records this metadata; the original data files are never copied or moved.
Product definitions and dataset documents: YAML/JSON documents that describe, respectively, a type of data (e.g. a Landsat surface reflectance product) and each individual dataset to be indexed (its extent, time, measurements, and file paths).
ODC Explorer: a web application for browsing what has been indexed: available products, spatial/temporal coverage, and dataset-level metadata.
Complementary tools: including datacube-ows (OGC WMS/WMTS/WCS web services), datacube-stats (large-scale statistical summaries), and STAC-related tooling for interoperability with the wider Earth observation ecosystem.

title: Open Data Cube (ODC) — Overview
text:
How the pieces fit together
A running ODC deployment is essentially the datacube-core software connected to a PostgreSQL/PostGIS database, with data indexed into it via product definitions and dataset documents. Once populated, the cube can be queried through the Python API, browsed through the Explorer, or served via OGC web services, all reading from the same underlying index.

The Installation and Quick Start pages walk through setting this up step by step.

title: Open Data Cube (ODC) — Overview
text:
Project and community
ODC is maintained as a community open-source project, with its source code, issue tracker, and documentation hosted on GitHub and Read the Docs. It is governed openly, with contributions from the agencies and research groups that operate the deployments listed above.

title: How to index new data into a DC?
text:
Once a datacube is deployed, the Earth observation archive keeps growing: new satellite scenes become available over time and need to be added to the existing index so they can be queried and analysed alongside the rest of the archive. Since the Nostradamus datacube uses a STAC datastore (the Planetary Computer catalog) as its data source, new scenes do not need to be prepared or described by hand: they can be indexed directly from the STAC catalog into an existing product.
In short, the procedure consists of searching the STAC catalog for new scenes matching a product, an area of interest, and a date range, then registering the matching STAC items into the corresponding ODC product already configured in the cube. This is done with the stac-to-dc command-line tool (part of odc-apps-dc-tools), which is already installed in the Nostradamus JupyterHub environment. Once indexed, the new scenes are immediately visible in the ODC Explorer and loadable through the Python API, exactly like the rest of the archive.
The steps below index new Landsat Collection 2 Level-2 scenes into the existing lsX_c2l2_sp product (see the Landsat page) as a concrete example.

title: How to index new data into a DC?
text:
Indexing new Landsat scenes: step-by-step

Open a Terminal in the Nostradamus JupyterHub (File > New > Terminal), where datacube and stac-to-dc are already available.
Check that the target product is already registered in the cube:
datacube product list | grep lsX_c2l2_sp
Search the Planetary Computer STAC catalog for new scenes and index them directly into that product, specifying the collection, an area of interest (bounding box), and a date range:
stac-to-dc \
  --catalog-href="https://planetarycomputer.microsoft.com/api/stac/v1/" \
  --collections="landsat-c2-l2" \
  --bbox="5.95,45.81,10.50,47.81" \
  --datetime="2026-01-01/2026-06-30" \
  --rename-product="lsX_c2l2_sp" \
  --update-if-exists
--rename-product maps the STAC collection (landsat-c2-l2) to the existing ODC product name (lsX_c2l2_sp), and --bbox/--datetime restrict the search to the area and period you need (adjust them to your own area of interest).







Note



Planetary Computer assets are served through short-lived signed URLs. If loading newly indexed scenes later fails with an access error, see the STAC datastore page for how signing is handled, or re-run the indexing step to refresh the references.



Check the command’s output: it reports how many datasets were added, failed, and skipped (already-indexed scenes are skipped, not duplicated).
Confirm the new scenes are indexed by checking the product’s extent in the ODC Explorer, at localhost/explorer/products/lsX_c2l2_sp: the temporal coverage should now include your new date range.
Alternatively, confirm it directly from a notebook using the Python API:
from datacube import Datacube

dc = Datacube(app="check-new-data")
data = dc.load(product="lsX_c2l2_sp", time=("2026-01-01", "2026-06-30"))
print(data.time.values)

section: What can a data cube be used for?
text:
What can a data cube be used for?
A data cube can support many different applications. The examples below are drawn from publications by Gregory Giuliani and Bruno Chatenoux (University of Geneva / UNEP-GRID Geneva), based on the Swiss Data Cube, an Open Data Cube deployment. For each reference, the indices computed from the datacube are indicated.

Chatenoux B., Richard J.-P., Small D., Röösli C., Wingate V., Poussin C., Rodila D., Peduzzi P., Steinmeier C., Ginzler C., Psomas A., Schaepman M., Giuliani G. (2021) — The Swiss Data Cube, Analysis Ready Data archive using Earth Observations of Switzerland, Scientific Data 8:295. Indices produced: NDVI, NDWI, EVI, GCI, LAI, MSI, ARI.
Poussin C., Massot A., Ginzler C., Weber D., Chatenoux B., Lacroix P., Piller T., Nguyen L., Giuliani G. (2021) — Drying conditions in Switzerland – Indication from a 35-year Landsat trend analysis of vegetation water content estimates to support SDGs, Big Earth Data. Index computed: NDWI (also referred to as NDMI), used as a proxy for vegetation water content and drought monitoring.
Obuchowicz C., Poussin C., Giuliani G. (2023) — Change in observed long-term greening across Switzerland – Evidence from a three decades NDVI time-series and its relationship with climate and land cover factors, Big Earth Data. Index computed: NDVI, used to track long-term vegetation greening trends.
Poussin C., Timoner P., Chatenoux B., Giuliani G., Peduzzi P. (2023) — Improved Landsat-based snow cover mapping accuracy using a spatiotemporal NDSI and generalised linear mixed model, Science of Remote Sensing 7:100078. Index computed: NDSI, used for snow cover mapping.
Cornut C., Ozainne S., Poussin C., Andenmatten R., Giuliani G. (2022) — Identifying areas of archaeological potential in the Swiss Alps using satellite-derived time-series of snow cover estimates, Remote Sensing Applications: Society and Environment 28:100838. Index computed: NDSI, used to derive snow cover duration/melt-out time-series.
Giuliani G., Chatenoux B., De Bono A., Rodila D., Richard J.-P., Allenbach K., Dao H., Peduzzi P. (2017) — Building an Earth Observations Data Cube: lessons learned from the Swiss Data Cube (SDC) on generating Analysis Ready Data (ARD), Big Earth Data 1:100–117. Indices discussed: NDVI, NDWI, as part of the ARD generation and validation process.

title: How to retrieve data using the Python API?
section: Retrieving data with the Python API: step-by-step
text:
Retrieving data with the Python API: step-by-step

Open a Jupyter notebook in the Nostradamus JupyterHub, where the datacube Python package is already installed and configured.
Connect to the datacube:
from datacube import Datacube

dc = Datacube(app="retrieve-data-example")
Check that the target product is available, and inspect its measurements (bands):
dc.list_products()
dc.list_measurements().loc["s2_l2a"]
Optionally, check what data actually exists for your area and period before loading it, using find_datasets(). This avoids launching a costly load() call over an area with no coverage:
datasets = dc.find_datasets(
    product="s2_l2a",
    x=(6.1, 6.2),
    y=(46.2, 46.3),
    time=("2024-01-01", "2024-06-30"),
)
print(len(datasets), "datasets found")
Load the data for a given product, area, time range, and set of measurements:
data = dc.load(
    product="s2_l2a",
    x=(6.1, 6.2),
    y=(46.2, 46.3),
    time=("2024-01-01", "2024-06-30"),
    measurements=["red", "nir"],
    output_crs="EPSG:32631",
    resolution=(-10, 10),
)
data
x/y define the bounding box of your area of interest (longitude/latitude by default), time the date range, and measurements the bands to load. output_crs and resolution control the projection and pixel size of the resulting grid.







Note



The first call to dc.load() over a new area or product can take a while, since it triggers reprojection and resampling across every matching scene. Restricting measurements to only the bands you need, and narrowing x/y/time, significantly speeds this up.



Explore the result: data is returned as an xarray Dataset with x, y, and time dimensions, plus one variable per requested measurement:
print(data.dims)
print(list(data.data_vars))
Use the loaded data directly with the Python scientific stack — for example, computing and plotting an NDVI time-series:
ndvi = (data.nir - data.red) / (data.nir + data.red)
ndvi.mean(dim=["x", "y"]).plot()

For the full list of products and measurements available in the Nostradamus datacube, see the Data sources used page.
